name: Healthcare Administration
notes: Competency areas and item counts taken from the Florida FBLA Healthcare Administration event page (https://www.flfbla.org/fbla-event-health-care-administration): 100 multiple-choice questions, 50 minutes, 8 knowledge areas (15/10/10/15/10/10/15/15). The official fbla.org event page and 2025-26 guideline PDF returned HTTP 403 / 404 to the fetch tool, so they could not be read directly. FBLA's 2025-26 high school event list (https://www.fbla.org/media/2025/05/25-26-HS-CE-List.pdf) confirms Healthcare Administration is an individual objective test for grades 9-12. Sub counts are approximate to the Florida weights: actual counts are Organizations 15, Finances 14, Staffing 10, Strategy 11, Technology 10, Billing 14, Policy 16, Communication 10 (billing and finance run high because revenue-cycle questions were kept). The Florida page's knowledge-area list omits Healthcare Organizations and Structure, but its item counts include it, so it is kept here. Questions are original and use U.S. law (HIPAA, Stark, Anti-Kickback, EMTALA, CMS, OSHA). Answer keys re-verified 2026-10-11 (all 100 re-solved); giveaway wording, weak distractors, and a few sub tags fixed.

questions.q: Which type of managed care plan requires members to select a primary care provider and generally requires referrals to see specialists?
questions.explain: HMOs use a primary care gatekeeper and typically require referrals; PPOs allow self-referral and out-of-network care at higher cost.

questions.q: A hospital receives a fixed amount per member per month to cover all necessary care for a defined population, regardless of how many services each member uses. What is this payment method called?
questions.explain: Capitation shifts financial risk to the provider. The trap is case rate, which pays a fixed amount per episode rather than per member.

questions.q: A hospital owned and run by a county or state is classified as which type?
questions.explain: Public hospitals are owned and run by government entities; investor-owned hospitals are for-profit, and voluntary hospitals are nonprofit.

questions.q: An accountable care organization (ACO) differs from traditional fee-for-service primarily because ACO participants:
choices: Are paid separately for each visit and procedure, with no shared risk
Receive a fixed monthly payment per member with no quality targets
Share in savings or losses tied to cost and quality for an assigned population
Must directly employ every physician who participates in the ACO
questions.explain: ACOs are accountable for total cost and quality for an assigned population and can share savings (and in some tracks, losses). Per-procedure payment is fee-for-service, a flat per-member payment is capitation, and ACOs can be networks of independent practices.

questions.q: A hospital's case mix index (CMI) is used primarily to:
choices: Measure patient satisfaction with the discharge process
Calculate the percentage of staffed beds occupied
Gauge the average resource intensity of the patient mix
Track the number of emergency visits per year
questions.explain: CMI reflects the relative resource use of a patient mix. It is often confused with occupancy, which measures bed use.

questions.q: Which term describes a hospital's complete list of standard charges for every item and service, used as the starting point for billing?
questions.explain: The chargemaster is the hospital's master price list. A superbill is a superficially similar form used by physician offices.

questions.q: A community health center that receives federal grants, serves patients regardless of ability to pay, and is reimbursed under a special Medicare payment system is most likely a:
questions.explain: FQHCs receive HRSA grants, serve underserved populations, and are paid under a Medicare prospective payment system for clinic visits.

questions.q: Which long-term care setting provides round-the-clock care by licensed nurses and daily rehabilitation therapy for patients who no longer need hospital care?
questions.explain: Skilled nursing facilities provide daily skilled nursing and therapy. Assisted living focuses on custodial help with daily activities.

questions.q: Which payment method pays providers separately for every visit, test, and procedure, so revenue rises with volume?
questions.explain: Fee-for-service rewards volume. Bundled payments and pay-for-performance tie payment to episodes or outcomes instead.

questions.q: A hospital has an average daily census of 180 patients and 240 staffed beds. What is its occupancy rate?
questions.explain: Occupancy = 180 / 240 = 75%. Dividing the other way gives 133%, a common error.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation FTE stand for in healthcare staffing?
questions.explain: FTE converts part-time and full-time hours into full-time units, commonly 40 hours per week or 2,080 hours per year.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis, which factor is internal to the organization?
questions.explain: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external. Competitor pricing is an external factor.

questions.q: Under OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, what must an employer provide to employees with occupational exposure to blood?
choices: Protective equipment purchased by each employee
One training session at hire, with no annual refresher
The hepatitis B vaccine only after an exposure incident
Annual training and the hepatitis B vaccine at no cost to the employee
questions.explain: The standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) requires training at assignment and at least annually, hepatitis B vaccination offered at no cost within 10 working days of assignment, and employer-provided protective equipment. Each other choice breaks one of those rules.

questions.q: In SBAR communication, what does the letter B stand for?
questions.explain: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.

questions.q: Which leadership style involves making decisions after gathering input from staff while the leader keeps final authority?
questions.explain: Participative leaders consult staff before deciding. Autocratic leaders decide alone, and laissez-faire leaders step back.

questions.q: Which HL7 interoperability standard exchanges health data through RESTful APIs and modular resources, and is the newer alternative to HL7 version 2 messaging?
questions.explain: FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is the HL7 standard built on web APIs. DICOM handles imaging, NCPDP SCRIPT handles e-prescriptions, and X12 837 handles claims.

questions.q: A PACS system is primarily used to:
choices: Store, retrieve, and display medical images
questions.explain: PACS (picture archiving and communication system) manages medical images such as X-rays and CT scans.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an electronic health record (EHR)?
choices: A digital patient record that can be shared across providers and settings
A health record the patient creates and manages, such as a phone app
Practice management software that handles claims and billing
A digital chart used only inside one practice and not shared
questions.explain: An EHR is a digital clinical record built to be shared across providers and settings. A chart kept inside one practice is an EMR, a patient-managed record is a PHR, and claims software is practice management, not the EHR's main purpose.

questions.q: Which telehealth modality involves recording a patient's images or data and sending them to a specialist for later review?
questions.explain: Store-and-forward is asynchronous. Remote patient monitoring sends ongoing device readings, which is different.

questions.q: A payer denies a claim because the diagnosis code reported does not justify the procedure that was billed. Which denial category is this?
questions.explain: A medical necessity denial means the documented diagnosis does not justify the service. Eligibility denials concern coverage status.

questions.q: What is a deductible?
choices: The fee paid each time a service is received
The percentage of costs shared after the plan pays
The amount the insured pays before the plan begins paying covered services
The maximum an insurer pays in a year
questions.explain: The deductible is the out-of-pocket amount paid before coverage starts paying. Coinsurance is the percentage share, and copayment is the fixed fee.

questions.q: Coinsurance is best defined as:
choices: A fixed dollar amount the insured pays at each visit
The amount the insured pays before the plan begins to pay
The insured's percentage share of costs after the deductible
The monthly premium the insured pays to keep coverage
questions.explain: Coinsurance is a percentage of allowed charges the insured pays after the deductible. A fixed per-visit amount is a copayment, and the amount paid before coverage starts is the deductible.

questions.q: What is a copayment?
choices: A fixed amount paid at the time of service
The annual maximum the insured must pay
A discount from the provider's chargemaster
questions.explain: A copayment is a fixed dollar amount, often due at the visit. Coinsurance is a percentage.

questions.q: Which federal law requires hospitals with emergency departments to screen and stabilize patients regardless of ability to pay?
questions.explain: EMTALA is the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act. HITECH covers health IT and breach rules, CLIA covers lab testing, and ERISA covers employee benefit plans.

questions.q: Modifier 25 appended to an E/M code indicates:
choices: A significant, separately identifiable E/M service on the same day as a procedure
An unrelated E/M visit during a procedure's postoperative period
A distinct procedure performed at a separate site or session
A service delivered by real-time audio and video telehealth
questions.explain: Modifier 25 reports a significant, separately identifiable E/M service on the same day as a procedure. The other choices describe modifier 24 (unrelated E/M in a postoperative period), 59 (distinct procedural service), and 95 (synchronous telehealth).

questions.q: Which HR process verifies a clinician's licenses, certifications, and training before hiring or privileging?
questions.explain: Credentialing verifies qualifications. Onboarding is the later process of integrating a new hire.

questions.q: Employee turnover rate is calculated as:
choices: Hires during the period divided by average number of employees, times 100
Separations during the period divided by average number of employees, times 100
Separations during the period divided by hires during the period, times 100
Employees at year-end divided by employees at year-start, times 100
questions.explain: Turnover rate = separations divided by average headcount, multiplied by 100. Hires divided by headcount is a hire rate, and comparing separations with hires or year-end with year-start headcount is not turnover.

questions.q: Which training method is most effective for teaching staff a new electronic health record system?
choices: Emailing staff the vendor's user manual to read before go-live
Hands-on practice in a test environment with super-user support
A single classroom lecture months before go-live
A short webinar on go-live day with no practice time
questions.explain: Hands-on practice in a training environment, backed by super-users, builds real skill. Reading a manual, a lecture held long before go-live, or a short webinar gives staff little practice.

questions.q: Performance appraisal feedback is most effective when it is:
choices: Saved for the annual review so it is delivered all at once
Based on the manager's overall impression of the employee
Focused on ranking the employee against coworkers
Specific, timely, and tied to documented goals
questions.explain: Effective feedback is specific, timely, and linked to documented goals. Saving it for one annual meeting, relying on general impressions, or ranking against peers makes it less useful.

questions.q: Which federal law requires covered employers with at least 50 employees to provide eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave per year?
questions.explain: The FMLA sets the 50-employee threshold and 12-week leave. The ADA applies at 15 employees, which is a common mix-up.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation PTO stand for in staffing benefits?
questions.explain: PTO (paid time off) combines vacation and sick time in one bank.

questions.q: Orientation for new clinical staff typically includes which element that accreditation standards expect?
choices: A probationary pay rate for the first 90 days
Competency verification for the assigned role
Enrolment in the organization's retirement plan
questions.explain: Accreditors such as The Joint Commission expect orientation to include verifying that staff are competent for their role. Pay, benefits, and contracts are HR paperwork, not accreditation requirements.

questions.q: A hospital's mission statement primarily answers which question?
choices: Where do we want to be in ten years?
What are our quarterly sales targets?
questions.explain: Mission describes purpose; vision describes the desired future state.

questions.q: The PDSA cycle stands for:
questions.explain: PDSA (Plan-Do-Study-Act) is a continuous improvement cycle used in quality work.

questions.q: The balanced scorecard evaluates organizational performance across which four perspectives?
choices: Financial, customer, internal processes, learning and growth
questions.explain: Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard uses those four perspectives. SWOT and PDSA are different tools.

questions.q: A hospital wants to reduce process variation in a surgical checklist using the DMAIC phases. Which quality approach uses DMAIC?
questions.explain: Six Sigma uses Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control (DMAIC) to reduce defects and variation.

questions.q: In Lean methodology, which of the following is an example of waste?
questions.explain: Waiting is one of the classic Lean wastes. The other options are tools or practices that support flow.

questions.q: Which term describes a clear statement of what an organization hopes to become in the future?
questions.explain: Vision is the future aspiration. Mission is current purpose and objectives are measurable targets.

questions.q: Porter's five forces analysis is used to assess:
choices: An organization's internal strengths and weaknesses
The quality of patient care processes
Competitive intensity and profitability of an industry
questions.explain: The five forces assess rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, supplier power, and buyer power within an industry. Internal strengths and weaknesses belong to a SWOT analysis.

questions.q: Kotter's eight-step change model begins with which step?
questions.explain: Urgency comes first in Kotter's model. Consolidating gains and anchoring change come later.

questions.q: Which accrediting body surveys and accredits U.S. hospitals and other healthcare organizations?
questions.explain: The Joint Commission is a private accreditor. CMS sets Medicare rules, and the OIG investigates fraud.

questions.q: Which type of hospital is a rural facility with no more than 25 inpatient beds that Medicare pays on a reasonable-cost basis?
questions.explain: Critical access hospitals are designated rural facilities limited to 25 inpatient beds (42 CFR 485.620) that Medicare pays at 101% of reasonable cost.

questions.q: A physician group in which members share patient care responsibilities and bill under one tax ID is best described as a:
questions.explain: A group practice shares overhead and often a single billing identity. A solo practice has one physician owner.

questions.q: In a hospital's organizational chart, which role reports directly to the board of directors and is responsible for overall operations?
questions.explain: The CEO is the top executive and reports to the board. Other executives report to the CEO.

questions.q: A patient does not have to choose a primary care provider, can see specialists without a referral, and can use out-of-network providers at a higher cost-sharing rate. Which plan type does the patient most likely have?
questions.explain: PPOs need no gatekeeper or referrals and cover out-of-network care at higher cost. POS plans usually require a primary care provider and referrals, and EPOs and HMOs generally do not cover out-of-network care.

questions.q: Which type of hospital primarily serves patients with mental illness?
questions.explain: Psychiatric hospitals focus on mental health care. Rehabilitation hospitals focus on recovery from injury or illness.

questions.q: Which system tracks patient flow, bed availability, and discharge planning in real time?
questions.explain: Bed management systems track capacity and patient movement. The other systems serve different functions.

questions.q: In health information technology, what does the abbreviation HIE stand for?
questions.explain: HIE is the health information exchange, which allows secure sharing of records across organizations.

questions.q: Computerized provider order entry (CPOE) primarily reduces which risk?
questions.explain: CPOE replaces handwritten orders, reducing transcription and medication errors.

questions.q: Under the HIPAA Security Rule, which category of safeguards includes unique user IDs, audit controls, and automatic logoff?
questions.explain: Technical safeguards control access to electronic PHI. Administrative and physical safeguards cover policies and facilities.

questions.q: Which federal law is the primary privacy rule protecting individually identifiable health information?
questions.explain: HIPAA sets the Privacy, Security, and Breach Notification rules for protected health information.

questions.q: Under HIPAA, what is the minimum necessary standard?
choices: Patients must receive a minimum of 30 days notice
Providers must keep records for a minimum of 3 years
Staff must complete a minimum of 8 hours of training
Only the least PHI needed for a purpose may be used or disclosed
questions.explain: Minimum necessary limits PHI use and disclosure to what is needed for the purpose, with exceptions such as treatment.

questions.q: Which HIPAA rule requires covered entities to tell affected individuals, HHS, and sometimes the media when unsecured PHI has been improperly acquired or disclosed?
questions.explain: The Breach Notification Rule (under HITECH) sets the notice requirements. The Privacy Rule covers permitted uses and disclosures.

questions.q: What is a Notice of Privacy Practices?
choices: A form the patient signs to let records be released to a third party
A notice sent to patients after their PHI has been breached
A document explaining how a covered entity uses and discloses PHI and patients' rights
A list of every disclosure made of the patient's PHI
questions.explain: HIPAA requires covered entities to give patients a notice describing how PHI is used and disclosed and what rights patients have. The other choices describe an authorization, a breach notice, and an accounting of disclosures.

questions.q: Which federal program provides health coverage for low-income children and families and is jointly funded by federal and state governments?
questions.explain: Medicaid is jointly funded and run by states under federal rules. Medicare serves mainly people 65 and older and people with certain disabilities.

questions.q: Which federal law prohibits offering or receiving remuneration to induce referrals of business payable by federal healthcare programs?
questions.explain: The Anti-Kickback Statute is a criminal law. Stark is a civil self-referral law for physicians.

questions.q: Under MACRA, which program combines quality, cost, and improvement activities into a single payment adjustment for clinicians?
questions.explain: MIPS is the MACRA program that adjusts Medicare payments based on a composite performance score.

questions.q: Which federal act, signed in 2010, expanded health insurance coverage through Medicaid expansion and health insurance marketplaces?
questions.explain: The Affordable Care Act, signed in 2010, expanded coverage and created marketplaces. The Medicare Modernization Act added Part D in 2003.

questions.q: Which federal law requires employer group health plans to offer continued coverage after a qualifying job loss?
questions.explain: COBRA allows continuation of group coverage for a period after qualifying events such as job loss.

questions.q: Which activity do the federal CLIA regulations govern?
questions.explain: CLIA sets quality standards for laboratory testing on human specimens. FDA handles drugs and devices.

questions.q: Which CMS-adopted code set is used to report diagnoses for U.S. healthcare encounters?
questions.explain: ICD-10-CM is the U.S. diagnosis code set. CPT codes procedures, HCPCS Level II covers supplies and some services, and NDC identifies drugs.

questions.q: Which code set describes medical procedures and services and is maintained by the American Medical Association?
questions.explain: CPT (Current Procedural Terminology) is maintained by the AMA. ICD-10-PCS is used for inpatient procedures, and HCPCS Level II is maintained by CMS.

questions.q: Which claim form is used primarily by physicians and other professional providers?
questions.explain: The CMS-1500 is the professional claim form. The UB-04 is used by institutional providers such as hospitals.

questions.q: An explanation of benefits (EOB) is:
choices: A bill the provider sends the patient for a copayment
A provider's request for prior authorization from the payer
A payer's statement to the insured showing what was covered and paid
A provider's list of standard charges for each service
questions.explain: An EOB is a payer statement sent to the insured. It is not a bill, and the provider does not send it. The provider receives a remittance advice instead.

questions.q: Which term describes a claim that contains all necessary information and can be adjudicated without further investigation?
questions.explain: A clean claim passes edits without manual review. Pended claims need follow-up before processing.

questions.q: Which term refers to the amount a provider has agreed to accept from a payer for a service, which may be less than the billed charge?
questions.explain: The allowed amount is the contracted payment. Gross charges and chargemaster rates are the billed amounts.

questions.q: Prior authorization is:
choices: Approval from the payer before certain services are provided
A payment made after a claim denial
A patient's written consent to treatment
questions.explain: Prior authorization is payer approval before a service, often for high-cost procedures. Informed consent is a different concept.

questions.q: What does COB stand for in insurance billing?
questions.explain: Coordination of benefits determines which payer is primary when a patient has more than one plan.

questions.q: Days in accounts receivable is calculated as:
choices: (Accounts receivable divided by net credit revenue) times 365
Net credit revenue divided by accounts receivable
(Cash collected divided by gross charges) times 100
Accounts payable divided by operating expenses
questions.explain: Days in AR = accounts receivable divided by average daily net revenue (net revenue / 365), which shows how long collection takes. Choice B is the receivables turnover ratio, not days.

questions.q: A clinic has fixed costs of $120,000 per year, a price of $80 per visit, and a variable cost of $40 per visit. How many visits are needed to break even?
questions.explain: Break-even = fixed costs divided by contribution margin: 120,000 / (80 - 40) = 3,000 visits.

questions.q: Which accounting basis records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands?
questions.explain: Accrual accounting matches revenue and expenses to the period. Cash basis records only when cash moves.

questions.q: Which budget type is prepared from zero each year, requiring every expense to be justified?
questions.explain: Zero-based budgets require justification for each expense. Incremental budgets start from last year's amounts.

questions.q: A hospital reports gross patient charges of $5,000,000 and contractual allowances of $2,000,000. What is net patient service revenue before bad debt?
questions.explain: Net patient revenue = gross charges minus contractual allowances, or $3,000,000. Bad debt is handled separately.

questions.q: Which financial statement shows an organization's assets, liabilities, and net assets at a point in time?
questions.explain: The balance sheet (called the statement of financial position by nonprofits) is a snapshot. The income statement and statement of activities cover a period.

questions.q: Which term describes a payment model where a provider receives one predetermined payment for all services in an episode of care, including related follow-up?
questions.explain: Bundled payments cover an episode as one package. A fee schedule prices each service separately, and per diem pays a set amount per day.

questions.q: What does a budget variance measure?
choices: The change in patient volume from one year to the next
The rate at which staff leave the organization
The difference between budgeted and actual amounts
The share of claims denied by insurers
questions.explain: A variance is actual minus budget, showing where spending or revenue differed from plan.

questions.q: Which technique asks a patient to restate in their own words what they understood, to confirm comprehension?
questions.explain: Teach-back checks understanding without quizzing the patient. Closed questions often produce only yes or no answers.

questions.q: What is the best first step when a patient becomes upset about a bill?
choices: Transfer the patient to the billing supervisor right away
Explain the insurer's contract terms in detail
Listen actively and acknowledge the concern
Offer to write off the balance to end the conversation
questions.explain: Listening and acknowledging the concern de-escalates first. Transferring right away or launching into contract details skips that step, and an unapproved write-off can raise compliance issues.

questions.q: Which communication barrier occurs when medical jargon is used with a patient who does not understand the terms?
questions.explain: Jargon the listener does not understand is a semantic (language) barrier. Plain language and teach-back reduce it.

questions.q: A manager wants to resolve a conflict between two staff members with a solution that meets both parties' core interests. Which conflict-handling approach does this describe?
questions.explain: Collaboration seeks a win-win solution. Competition wins at the other party's expense, and accommodation gives in.

questions.q: Which document names a person to make medical decisions if the patient becomes unable to communicate?
choices: Durable power of attorney for healthcare
questions.explain: A healthcare power of attorney appoints a healthcare agent. A notice of privacy practices describes HIPAA rights.

questions.q: Which standard defines the structure of electronic medical claims submitted to payers in the United States?
questions.explain: The X12 837 transaction is the HIPAA standard for electronic healthcare claims.

questions.q: What does HIPAA stand for?
choices: Hospital Information Privacy and Access Act
Health Information Protection and Administration Act
Healthcare Insurance Payment and Access Act
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
questions.explain: HIPAA is the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996.

questions.q: A hospital is planning service expansion. Which of the following is an external threat in a SWOT analysis?
questions.explain: Threats are external. Reputation and leadership are internal strengths, and grant funding is an opportunity.

questions.q: Under the Patient Self-Determination Act, healthcare providers must:
choices: Ask adult patients whether they have an advance directive and document the answer
Require adult patients to sign an advance directive as a condition of admission
Have staff draft a living will for every patient who lacks one
Ask only patients over 65 about advance directives
questions.explain: PSDA requires participating providers to inform adults of their advance directive rights and document whether one exists. Care cannot be conditioned on having a directive, and staff are not required to draft one.

questions.q: Which type of listening involves restating the speaker's message in your own words to confirm understanding?
questions.explain: Reflective listening paraphrases and confirms the message, which supports empathy.

questions.q: Under the Joint Commission's National Patient Safety Goals, which action is used to verify patient identity?
choices: Asking the patient, 'Are you Maria Lopez?'
Asking the patient to state full name and date of birth
questions.explain: NPSG.01.01.01 requires at least two patient identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, stated by the patient. A room number is never an identifier, and a yes-or-no question invites a wrong yes.

questions.q: Which leadership theory suggests the best leadership style depends on the situation and the readiness of followers?
questions.explain: Situational leadership adapts directive and supportive behaviour to follower readiness.

questions.q: Which goal-setting method has managers and employees agree on specific goals together and later review results against them?
questions.explain: Management by objectives (MBO) sets shared goals and evaluates performance against them.

questions.q: Which revenue cycle step involves checking a patient's coverage before a visit?
questions.explain: Eligibility verification confirms active coverage and benefits before service, reducing denials.

questions.q: A hospital has annual operating expenses of $36 million and 90 days cash on hand. What is its approximate cash on hand?
questions.explain: Cash = 36,000,000 / 365 times 90, which is about $8.9 million.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an orientation checklist for new hires?
choices: Rate the employee's job performance for the year
Ensure required tasks, policies, and training are completed
Record the employee's benefit choices and pay rate
Replace the written job description for the role
questions.explain: An orientation checklist confirms that required onboarding tasks, policy reviews, and training are completed and documented. It is not an appraisal, a payroll record, or a job description.

questions.q: A nurse-to-patient ratio is best defined as:
choices: The number of nurses hired per patient admitted
The number of patients assigned to each nurse on a shift
The total hours worked by nurses per week
The ratio of nursing salaries to revenue
questions.explain: Nurse-to-patient ratio is a staffing standard for assignments per shift, which affects safety and quality.

questions.q: Cross-training staff primarily helps a healthcare organization by:
choices: Raising every employee's pay grade automatically
Reducing the licences staff are required to hold
Limiting each employee to one specialized task
Increasing staffing flexibility when coverage gaps occur
questions.explain: Cross-training lets staff cover other roles during absences or surges. It does not change pay grades or licensure rules, and it widens rather than narrows what each person can do.

questions.q: Which term describes money a healthcare organization expects to collect from patients and payers for services already provided?
questions.explain: Accounts receivable are amounts owed to the organization. Accounts payable are amounts it owes.

questions.q: What is a remittance advice?
choices: A patient's request to transfer records to a new provider
A payer's list of drugs covered under the plan
A payer's statement to the provider detailing claim payments
A notice reminding the patient of an upcoming appointment
questions.explain: The remittance advice (ERA or paper) shows what was paid and why adjustments were made.

questions.q: A claim is denied for timely filing. This means the:
choices: Patient was not eligible on the date of service
Claim was submitted after the payer's filing deadline
Service is not covered by the plan
questions.explain: Timely filing denials occur when claims arrive after the payer's deadline.

questions.q: Which technology helps a hospital track the real-time location of mobile medical equipment?
questions.explain: RFID tags let staff locate equipment such as infusion pumps and reduce search time.

questions.q: Under HIPAA, what is the latest a covered entity may notify HHS of a breach affecting 500 or more individuals?
questions.explain: Breaches affecting 500 or more individuals must be reported to HHS without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery (45 CFR 164.408).

questions.q: Which action best demonstrates empathy when communicating with a grieving family?
choices: Telling them you know exactly how they feel
Acknowledging their loss and allowing them to speak without rushing
Reassuring them that everything happens for a reason
Handing them a grief brochure and quickly leaving
questions.explain: Empathy means acknowledging the loss and giving the family time to speak. Claiming to know how they feel, offering cliches, or hurrying away all shut the conversation down.

vocab.def: A managed care plan that uses a network of providers, usually requires a primary care gatekeeper and referrals, and generally does not cover out-of-network care except emergencies.
A managed care plan that allows members to see network or out-of-network providers without referrals, at a higher cost for out-of-network care.
A group of providers that share responsibility for the cost and quality of care for a defined patient population, and may share savings or losses.
A community health center that receives federal grants, serves underserved populations regardless of ability to pay, and is paid under a Medicare prospective payment system.
A designated rural hospital with a limited number of inpatient beds that is reimbursed by Medicare on a cost basis.
A facility that provides 24-hour skilled nursing care and rehabilitation services for patients who no longer need hospital-level care.
A hospital's master list of standard charges for each item and service, used as the basis for billing.
A measure of the average resource intensity of a hospital's patient mix, used to adjust payment and compare performance.
A private, nonprofit organization that accredits hospitals and other healthcare organizations by surveying them against performance standards.
A payment method in which a provider receives a fixed amount per enrolled patient per period, regardless of the number of services used.
A payment method in which providers are paid for each service or unit of care delivered.
A payment model that pays one predetermined amount for all services in a defined episode of care.
A digital record of a patient's health information that can be shared across care settings and includes clinical data.
A network that allows authorized organizations to share patient health information electronically.
The ability of different health information systems to exchange and use data accurately and consistently.
Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, an HL7 standard that exchanges health data through modular resources and web APIs.
Picture archiving and communication system, which stores, retrieves, and displays medical images.
The delivery of clinical and related services at a distance using telecommunications technology.
An asynchronous telehealth method in which images or data are recorded and sent to a clinician for later review.
A system in which clinicians enter medical orders electronically, reducing transcription and medication errors.
The amount an insured person pays for covered services before the insurer begins paying.
A fixed dollar amount an insured person pays for a covered service, often at the time of care.
The percentage of allowed charges an insured person pays after the deductible has been met.
The most an insured person must pay in a plan year for covered services before the insurer pays 100 percent.
A statement from the payer explaining what was covered, what was paid, and what the patient may owe.
A payer document that explains the payment made on a claim and any adjustments or denials.
A claim with complete and accurate information that can be processed without manual review or investigation.
A payer's approval required before certain services are provided, to confirm medical necessity and coverage.
Current Procedural Terminology codes maintained by the AMA that describe medical, surgical, and diagnostic services.
The International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification, used in the U.S. to code diagnoses.
A CMS-maintained code set for supplies, drugs, and services not covered by CPT codes.
The standard claim form used by professional providers, such as physicians, to bill payers.
The standard claim form used by institutional providers, such as hospitals, to bill payers.
A process that determines which insurer is primary and which is secondary when a patient has more than one plan.
The maximum amount a payer agrees to pay a provider for a covered service under a contract.
Amounts owed to an organization for services provided but not yet collected.
The average number of days it takes to collect payment, calculated as accounts receivable divided by net credit revenue, times 365.
An accounting method that records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash movement.
The difference between budgeted and actual amounts for a revenue or expense line.
A budgeting method in which every expense must be justified from zero each budget period.
A financial statement that reports assets, liabilities, and net assets at a specific point in time.
The standard that a service is reasonable and needed to diagnose or treat a patient's condition, supported by documentation.
The verification of a clinician's licenses, certifications, education, and training before employment or privileging.
A unit that converts staff hours into full-time positions, commonly 40 hours per week.
The percentage of employees who leave during a period, calculated as separations divided by average headcount, times 100.
A formal review of an employee's work against defined expectations, typically used for feedback and development.
The process of introducing new staff to the organization, policies, and role-specific competencies.
A strategic planning tool that assesses internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats.
A statement of an organization's purpose and what it does for its stakeholders.
A statement describing the future state an organization hopes to achieve.
A performance framework that measures results across financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth perspectives.
A continuous improvement method of Plan, Do, Study, and Act, used to test and refine changes.
A data-driven quality method that uses the DMAIC phases to reduce process variation and defects.
A management approach that focuses on eliminating waste, such as waiting, in order to improve flow and value.
A framework that assesses industry competition through rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, and the bargaining power of suppliers and buyers.
A structured communication tool using Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation to convey clinical information.
A technique in which a patient restates information in their own words to confirm understanding.
A written document stating a person's wishes for medical treatment if they become unable to decide for themselves.
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, which sets federal standards for privacy and security of protected health information.
A HIPAA principle that limits use and disclosure of protected health information to the minimum needed for the intended purpose.
